item.title: Things That Turbo Pascal Is Smaller Than (2011)
item.description:
It's not about technology for its own sake. It's about being able to implement your ideas.

Turbo Pascal 3 for MS-DOS was released in September 1986. Being version 3, there were lesser releases prior to it and flashier ones after, but 3 was a solid representation of the Turbo Pascal experience: a full Pascal compiler, including extensions that it made it practical for commercial use, tightly integrated with an editor. And the whole thing was lightning fast, orders of magnitude faster at building projects than Microsoft's compilers.

The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable--the compiler and IDE--was 39,731 bytes. How does that stack up in 2011 terms? Here are some things that Turbo Pascal is smaller than, as of October 30, 2011:

The minified version of jquery 1.6 (90,518 bytes).

The yahoo.com home page (219,583 bytes).

The image of the white iPhone 4S at apple.com (190,157 bytes).

zlib.h in the Mac OS X Lion SDK (80,504 bytes).

The touch command under OS X Lion (44,016 bytes).

Various vim quick reference cards as PDFs. (This one is 47,508 bytes.)

The compiled code for the Erlang R14B02 parser (erl_parse.beam, 286,324 bytes).

The Wikipedia page for C++ (214,251 bytes).

(If you liked this, you might like A Personal History of Compilation Speed.)

item.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
item.description:
All AI-generated code should be Open Source

This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

item.title: Emacs Is My Browser
item.description:
In my ever-increasing desire to use emacs as my sole computing environment, I have started to take browsing the web inside it far more seriously. Where I previously had thought EWW to be a niceity but far from capable, after using it for a few days it seems to be useable for about 85-90% of use cases - even on the javascript riddled hellhole that is the internet.

Why?#

I have seen in my own use of the modern browser (chromium/firefox) that it is far too easy to get distracted - too easy to get off track and fall down rabbit holes that take over my day. There are infinite suggestions as to how I should spend my time, uncountable shiny objects that take my eye off the prize that is Creativity and Depth. This has been momentously negated with EWW (or any terminal browser, lynx or browsh for the non-emacs users).

In addition to this, my belief is that we should make strides toward leaving behind Layer 8 of the internet - the limiting frontends of social platforms and locked away corners of the net that limit actual discourse (Discord, I’m looking at you). We have given up far too much to big tech platforms, and gotten nothing of value in return, to the point that many now think the internet is dying.

The internet is just a delivery mechanism, and for people that see it for what it really is, the internet has never been more alive. I truly recommend using the internet as if it was 1999.

Even on my phone, I’ve stopped using javascript frontends and embraced using eww in emacs (in termux), only falling back to fennec for about 5-10% of usecases:

I find this way of using the internet far higher in signal than any other method, allowing me to look up information, read documentation, and produce more.

How I am doing this#

For the uninitiated, emacs ships with EWW (Emacs Web Wowser) permitting you to browse the web with image and gif (when did gifs die, I almost never see them these days!) support directly inside Emacs.

I have some sane defaults that permit ease of use such as using B for back, U for yanking url at point, and a few built in functions.

Hitting R will invoke eww readable which is similar to reader mode in firefox, removing headers and footers and focusing in on the text on page. Useful.

You can send the page to your default browser with &. If a page doesn’t render nicely, this is a good fallback.

D will download images locally, b goes back a page, a will save bookmarks. All of this makes browsing in eww truly enjoyable.

I have also set .pdf to open in emacs, .mp4 and youtube/video hosting links to open in mpv, and gopher/gemini links to open in elpher. Elpher is the EWW for the gopher and gemini protocols, the smolweb that is all signal and no noise.

EWW uses Shr to render html, so you will see some callouts to that in my configuration below:

My browser.el setup:#

Here’s how I have configured EWW to work in my Emacs configuration:

My default search engine is my own Searx instance, a privacy respecting frontend that amalgamates all other search engines.

Limitations#

You will not be watching youtube videos or reading Tweets (x.com is adversarial to non-JS supported browsers). You will not be using social media, nor will you be logging into any platforms. You will not be doing your online banking, filling in government forms, or viewing client portals.

The usecase is quick web searches, documentation, and reading blogs generally. Once more, hitting & in any web page will bring up your default browser to continue your session in chromium or firefox when you do run into pages that don’t work well in EWW.

Conclusion#

I have reverted all my url functions to default to browsing in EWW, so any web interaction must first go through EWW. This has encouraged me to deeply consider what I am doing online first and foremost, and then only falling back to a modern browser when needed. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much I am able to do inside emacs, and continue to move toward using it as my computing environment in perpetuity.

As always, God bless, and until next time.

item.title: Clice v1.0 Released: Welcome to Modern C++
item.description:
clice recently hit 1,000 commits, a special milestone for the project. Since July 19, 2026, clice has been shipping nightly builds and going through roughly four months of alpha testing, with a huge number of bugs fixed thanks to real-world feedback from early users. Over the same stretch, I built a rigorous testing system for clice and ran extensive tests across many real open-source projects, tracking down and fixing the issues they uncovered. What does that mean? Every core feature is now stable, and you rarely run into problems in day-to-day use. So I think the time is right to ship the first stable release. The project looks very different today from where it stood two years ago in Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, and this is probably the first time I’m promoting it widely, so please let me introduce it to you once again! This is the project I have poured the past two and a half years into, the work I am proudest of, the one that has excited me the most and left me sad and anxious more times than I can count, and the most ambitious thing I have taken on in my short life.

What is clice?

In short, clice is a C/C++ language server written in modern C++, but it’s more than just a language server. It is still built on LLVM/Clang, but unlike clangd and ccls, which are also Clang-based, clice was redesigned from the ground up to fix architectural problems that have gone unsolved in those servers for years. It is written entirely in C++23 and serves as an example of modern C++ best practices in its own right, with all the major modern C++ features coming together remarkably well:

Written entirely with C++20 coroutines, using our own libuv-based structured-concurrency async library for intricate asynchronous logic. It is a complex concurrent program running an event loop on the main thread while coordinating both multiple processes (IPC) and multiple threads. Written entirely with C++20 named modules and C++23 import std, and fully self-hosted: module wrappers for third-party libraries are generated automatically by clice modularize, and clice runs smoothly on its own codebase to provide module-aware language services. Uses static reflection built on templates and C++20 concepts for all serialization and deserialization across formats, including TOML, JSON, bincode, blob, and command-line arguments, with Rust-macro-like declarative annotations and zero boilerplate. Data-oriented code design throughout, with almost no virtual functions outside the callback interfaces Clang requires. Makes heavy use of modern C++ APIs like std::format, std::expected, std::ranges, and std::views, steering clear of outdated legacy C++98/11 APIs. A completely hermetic, reproducible build powered by Bazel, compiled with the unified xclang toolchain for a consistent cross-platform cross-compilation workflow. Compiled binaries are heavily optimized (PGO + LTO), and build artifacts depend on nothing beyond system libraries.

People are always debating whether modern C++ features like modules are actually ready for real work. clice’s answer is: yes, of course, completely usable! They hold up for complex software like clice, with hundreds of thousands of lines of code. Maybe this is what the modern C++ we have been hoping for looks like. That said, the surrounding ecosystem really is inconvenient enough right now that getting this whole workflow running end to end took a huge amount of effort on my part to track issues and adapt everything.

 Language Server

Here is an overview of clice’s main features:

Multi-process compilation: clice compiles code in a process pool modeled after modern web browsers, whereas clangd uses multithreading. Why multiple processes? Because C++ is simply too complex, and on certain corner cases the compiler can easily crash or leak memory. That is especially true for incomplete code in the middle of editing: a huge downstream user base tests compilers on complete code, while very few people test them on half-written code, where the compiler mostly falls back on best-effort heuristics. In clangd, a compiler crash takes down the whole server and forces a restart. In clice, compilation happens in isolated child processes: losing one worker does not affect the rest of the server, so go-to-definition, highlighting, and other services keep working. It also makes it much easier to manage memory usage and schedule compilation priorities, cutting down on unnecessary resource consumption.

Modules and shared caching: clice has full support for C++20 named modules. All you need is a compile_commands.json containing all module files, and clice scans dependencies on its own and lazily builds required modules on demand, regardless of your build system or compiler, with full support for module completion, highlighting, go-to-definition, hover, and more. Built PCHs and PCMs are also cached on local disk for reuse across sessions. By comparison, clangd offers only very limited module support and no persistent cache.

Compilation context: clice has full support for non-self-contained files, and more generally for the concept of a compilation context. You can explicitly pick the active context of a file: a specific compile command for a source file, or a specific inclusion site for a header. When you open a non-self-contained file, clice detects its context automatically, so it works out of the box. More broadly, it also supports grouping compile commands into build configurations, letting you switch between, say, debug and release.

Better template support: clice implements a DFS pseudo instantiator that infers what many dependent names resolve to without needing concrete template arguments for a full instantiation. When a template has been instantiated once, clice also draws on that instantiation to power language features, such as completing on auto parameters of a lambda passed to a ranges call. On top of that, clice treats a template as a duck-typed interface and each instantiation as one of its implementations, much like a virtual function and its overrides: Go to Implementation on a dependent call inside a template lists the functions it actually calls across every instantiation, and Find References and Call Hierarchy work the same way.

Out-of-the-box experience: Most projects need nothing more than a compile_commands.json. clice ships with built-in environment probing for 50+ toolchains, covering nvcc, MSYS2, Cygwin, zigcc, and more, automatically handling mismatches between your actual compiler and Clang. You don’t have to manually add piles of compiler flags to a config file the way you do with clangd.

Beyond these main features, clice also fixes a long list of smaller clangd issues that have gone untouched for years across semantic highlighting, folding, hover, and more. If you’re interested, give it a try and see what surprises you find. Overall, clice surpasses clangd in ease of use, feature support, and performance. You can install the clice extension in VS Code and other editors and start using it right now.

Command Line

Besides running as a language server, clice can also be used from the CLI to access its language features directly. Currently supported subcommands include:

clice index: Builds a persistent index for the entire project ahead of time and supports resuming interrupted runs, so your editor starts warm as soon as you open the project. clice lint: Built-in clang-tidy runner that checks translation units concurrently across a process pool and merges duplicate diagnostics from headers; pass --index to reuse the same parse pass to build the index along the way. clice format: A wrapper around clang-format that automatically finds files to format from your config file or CDB and formats them efficiently in parallel. clice command: Shows the effective compile command for a file after rule rewrites and toolchain probing, or converts compile_commands.json into resolved -cc1 commands for other Clang tools. clice query: Reads the on-disk index directly without starting a server and outputs symbol definitions, references, call graphs, inheritance hierarchies, and file dependencies as JSON. clice refactor: Rewrites source files directly from the persistent index without recompiling, supporting project-wide symbol and macro renaming as well as batch renames in one pass via --spec. clice analyze: Outputs project-structure JSON from the index to guide refactoring; for example, analyze modules analyzes module dependencies and cycles across directories and lists code patterns that stand in the way of modularization. clice modularize: Automatically wraps third-party libraries used by a project as C++20 modules without modifying any source files; following the split analyze proposes, it can also rewrite the project’s own code into module units, turning headers into partitions and #include into import. clice used it to modularize itself. The story behind it

That wraps up the feature tour. Next, I want to talk about the story behind the project, some of its design decisions, and my own thoughts and struggles along the way, especially now, in the age of AI.

Why not improve clangd?

First, why start a new project instead of improving clangd? That is the question I get asked most often. There are several reasons. I discussed some of them in my earliest post, and today those problems are even easier to see firsthand:

Maintenance and staffing: At root, clangd has been effectively unmaintained since around 2024. That sounds surprising. How could a tool used by hundreds of thousands of developers have no one maintaining it? I stumbled onto this fact in 2024 when I was getting ready to submit a PR to clangd for better code completion inside templates. From what I understand, it ties back to a shift in Google’s C++ strategy. Before that, clangd was maintained mainly by several Google engineers, and around 2024 Google started scaling back its investment in C++ (Clang); clangd was deemed good enough for Google’s internal needs, and those engineers were reassigned elsewhere. Since then, clangd has lacked any real long-term maintainers. Only Nathan Ridge has been answering questions unpaid in his spare time, purely out of passion, and one person only has so much bandwidth, making it nearly impossible to handle large PRs. That is why clangd’s C++20 modules PR dragged on for nearly a year, and even today it still isn’t really usable on large projects, with plenty of flaws and nobody working on them. Earlier this year, in 2026, Clang’s lead maintainer Aaron Ballman recognized the problem and posted a call for help on the community forum, saying clangd is very close to unmaintained, with a heavy backlog of PRs and issues, and hoping to find new community maintainers; otherwise clangd could eventually be removed from the LLVM project.

Scale of the code changes: As mentioned at the start, clice introduces many new architectural ideas, such as multi-process compilation. Implementing those inside clangd would come close to rewriting clangd. Nobody is going to review and accept changes of that size. Self-hosting with modules would also require sweeping changes to LLVM’s build system, which I will go into in detail when I introduce xclang later.

LLVM repository constraints: clice relies on a lot of third-party libraries for better performance and user experience, such as libuv, simdjson, and tomlplusplus. To keep builds simple, LLVM requires the repository to remain self-contained, so pulling in that many third-party libraries is out of the question. You would either have to rewrite and port them into LLVM or put up with worse ergonomics and lower performance. On top of that, a language server is not a standalone project: it also includes extensions and adapters for different editors. Keeping them in the same repo as the server makes maintenance much easier, and LLVM would be just as unlikely to accept that editor code (spanning Rust, Lua, TypeScript, and so on). For long-term maintainability and our core goals, a separate repository was unavoidable.

So in mid-2024, I started looking into how to design and write a new language server. At the end of 2024, I published Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, setting out clice’s core goals and kicking off development in earnest.

How did we get here?

Next, let’s talk about how clice was built. How did it get to its current state? Over the past two and a half years, at a rough guess, I have put nearly 3,000 hours into this project. Even that number doesn’t really tell the story, because clice became part of my life. It was always on my mind, like eating or sleeping: there wasn’t a moment when I wasn’t turning over some problem related to it. Development broke down into roughly four stages:

Mid-2024 to early 2025: I spent this period studying Clang and clangd’s codebase and internals. Anyone who has looked through my older blog posts will know I am a longtime template metaprogramming enthusiast, familiar with C++ and its implementation details down to language-lawyer territory. During this phase I settled on clice’s core goals and overall design, and put together an initial demo. I was a third-year undergrad at the time: I would wake up and start coding right away, skip lunch, walk out to the McDonald’s outside the campus gate when I got hungry, and put in 8 to 10 hours a day.

Early 2025 to early 2026: I originally expected to ship a usable version of clice fairly quickly during this stage. Instead, progress went much slower than I expected, and it remained a long way from production-ready. Looking back, there were a few main reasons:

Above all, time. I had assumed I would keep putting in 8 to 10 hours a day like before. My undergraduate major was chemistry, though, and everything I knew about programming was self-taught. Even though I had plenty of C++ experience and had participated in GSoC, I lacked specific “domain knowledge.” To find a job, I spent most of 2025 interning and picking up a new field (unrelated to C++ frontends), while also dealing with university chores and everything involved in graduating. The hours I had left for clice shrank drastically compared to my earlier assumptions, so progress naturally slowed down. Getting the project genuinely production-ready also took far more than the core architecture. It meant working through countless corner cases of C++ syntax alongside subtle cross-platform differences: URI parsing, file paths and file uniqueness, OS-level quirks, and so on. The workload turned out to be much bigger than I had imagined. I also have a bit of an obsessive streak and dislike band-aid solutions that barely get by, so to build things the way I wanted I ended up reinventing quite a few wheels, covering serialization, IPC/LSP, async, and more. Had I chosen Rust at the start, development might have taken considerably less time, since those pieces already existed in the Rust ecosystem and had been thoroughly proven in other language servers. Still, writing a C++ language server in Rust felt odd, and it would have ruled out self-hosting, so I didn’t go that route. Lack of experience scheduling and managing complex software. Even with so much work on the table, several early contributors were already interested in the project and willing to put real time into helping write code. Unfortunately, I had very little teamwork experience back then (being completely self-taught and only three years into programming altogether), so I failed to turn that interest into effective contributions. That sank in much deeper once I started working in industry: 3 or 4 of my coworkers can split up responsibilities, stand up a project from scratch in 2 to 3 months, and ship it to production, whereas I had poor instincts for project planning and mostly just wrote whatever was on my mind at the moment. Open-source volunteer bandwidth can’t be compared to a full-time job, of course, yet the truth is I didn’t do a great job of building a community or pushing the project forward.

Early 2026 to July 2026: The turning point came when coding agents led by Claude Opus 4.6 started catching on. I began using agents to help with the mountain of tedious detail work and painful cross-platform debugging, and found they were remarkably good at it. During this stretch I did a sweeping cleanup of the existing codebase and established the prototype of clice as it stands today. As agents grew stronger, I handed them increasingly complex tasks and kept moving the project forward rapidly. It was an exciting period: I could finally stop burning hours on tedious details and focus on architecture and feature work. At the same time, it hit me that coding agents were only going to keep getting stronger. If humans stop writing code altogether in the future, what point does a language server even have? That pushed me to start designing and building clice’s CLI features.

July 2026 to present: By July I felt the timing was right to put out early test builds and iterate based on real user feedback. Core language server features were already in place and fully usable day to day, though still short of everything I had originally envisioned, so I threw myself into building out the rest of that vision, tuning performance, and fixing bugs. In October, I started planning clice’s modular self-hosting. That was a remarkably complicated undertaking, because C++ module support today is a long, painful story:

CMake supports modules, yet if implementation units importing a module use different compile flags, CMake forks a separate compilation of the module even when those flags don’t affect PCM compatibility. CMake also has no built-in compilation cache, which matters a lot for CI; normally we reach for ccache to solve that, except ccache doesn’t support modules. clice has a demanding platform matrix: six combinations across Windows/Linux/macOS × ARM64/x64, plus ASan builds, prebuilt LLVM/Clang binaries to speed up CI, C++23 import std, and build artifacts that depend only on system libraries rather than extra shared libraries so everything works out of the box for users.

I surveyed the options extensively, and the answer was that an out-of-the-box setup for this simply did not exist in open source, and most open-source C++ module projects don’t have build requirements nearly this involved. After thinking it through carefully, I built xclang, inspired by zigcc, to give every target platform a unified cross-compilation experience, and paired it with Bazel (which includes built-in build caching) to solve the build problem for good. Going one step further, I wrote clice modularize to automatically generate module wrappers for every third-party library we depend on, completing clice’s self-hosted modularization! That probably makes clice one of the most complex open-source C++ projects using modules today.

Alongside all of this, I ran extensive fuzz testing across many open-source projects and fixed a huge number of bugs, bringing clice to genuine production readiness!

What about agents?

As I mentioned earlier, I designed a CLI interface for clice so that it would still hold some value in the agent era. An obvious idea is replacing grep with clice query: it is more accurate and uses fewer tokens. That is true, except exact symbol lookup requires indexing the whole project first, which takes a very long time. grep is imprecise, sure, yet 2 or 3 grep calls are usually enough to find the target, and the extra text grep pulls back isn’t necessarily a bad thing for helping an agent understand the codebase. Put plainly, most of this CLI isn’t actually all that useful. The part that really earns its keep is probably clice modularize: if you ask an agent to modularize a project on its own, it spins up a swarm of subagents and writes custom scripts to pull off the migration, which is both slow and expensive. Giving the agent clice modularize to assist the migration works much better. LLMs are trained first and foremost for generality, and what they do best is writing and combining scripts to generalize across problems. As things stand, only highly specialized tools still carry real value; otherwise you are usually better off letting the LLM compose its own scripts.

As agents keep getting stronger, especially with models led by Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, the cost of building complex software keeps falling, and 10x or even 100x the productivity of the past is well within reach. Over on X, you can see plenty of people asking Claude in a single sentence to rewrite the TypeScript compiler in another programming language and getting better performance out of it. Surprising at first glance, yet completely reasonable when you think about it. Software written in the past was bounded by human time, cost, and skill, so codebases inevitably accumulated lots of suboptimal code paths. When humans optimize performance, we go after the main bottlenecks, whereas an agent can tirelessly optimize every path until the small wins add up. Refactoring also often produces a better architecture than existing code; rewriting or refactoring software was just too expensive to justify before. In the foreseeable future, then, most code may be written entirely by agents, humans may stop writing code and even reading it (which is already happening now), and language servers may have no reason to exist at all. Agents might even invent programming languages better suited to themselves: compilation and interpretation themselves have often become the bottleneck in the agent loop, and agents already have the ability to optimize that underlying infrastructure; they just haven’t started yet. Ideally, every stage of the agent loop should be something the agent itself can improve and speed up, compilers and toolchains included.

To be continued

That is a sad reality, and in an era like this it means the effort I poured into clice over the past two and a half years is unlikely to have the lasting meaning I first imagined. Every time I dwell on it, I slip into a dark mood, bordering on nihilism. I can’t help asking myself: thousands of hours and a lot of money, and what was it all for?

Because I taught myself programming off the beaten path without a CS degree, I got used early on to the cycle of finding my own goals, defining problems, solving them, and then looking for the next goal. Interest alone only sustains me for a little while; sticking with something for the long haul takes some deeper “meaning” or “vision” behind it, ideally one I defined for myself. And now that meaning is fading away. So over the past few months, I started pushing myself relentlessly. The more those thoughts crept in, the harder I used agents to drive the project forward, trying to finish it before it lost its meaning altogether.

Imagine an alternate timeline where coding agents never took off. clice wouldn’t be nearly as complete as it is today, of course, yet I would have slowly gained experience, learned how to collaborate and plan work, built a community around it, and watched clice move forward slowly and steadily. Except the SOTA models have already been trained. Models like Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are real, and whether AI is a bubble or not, they aren’t going away. Software becoming cheap is already an undeniable fact.

We have to face reality, so what mindset should we bring to all of this? My thinking has shifted again recently, though honestly neither my mental state nor my daily life is in a great place right now. Pouring yourself too deeply into one thing naturally takes a heavy toll when it doesn’t turn out the way you hoped. Still, if you zoom out over a longer stretch of time, what does it really amount to? Even if I had done nothing at all for these two and a half years, so what? There is plenty of life ahead. I know that in principle, yet letting go is hard, especially when this project has been part of my life for over two years. As I mentioned in an earlier post, graduating from college never really felt real to me, because the rhythm of my life barely changed afterward: apart from my job, it was just this project. Something has to change eventually, though. I can treat clice as my graduation project: my real graduation project, not one from the chemistry major I never really liked. And that’s enough. I don’t need to force a grander meaning onto it. This graduation project has met every single goal I set two years ago, and exceeded them by a wide margin. It stands on its own as the best illustration of modern C++, neatly bringing together everything I studied about C++ in college. If on top of that it can be helpful to people just learning to program or curious about modern C++, that is plenty.

So this post is a kind of ritual for me. I need to step out of my old life and look for other things worth doing, maybe things outside code. I will keep maintaining clice, just not at the intensity I used to; practically everything worth building is already built anyway, so from here on it will mostly be incremental optimizations and bug fixes based on user feedback. In times like these, it is hard to say what the right path is, or what you ought to be doing. Nobody knows what will happen next week, let alone next year, or how far AI will actually go. I think it is time to rest for a while so I don’t burn out, and have the energy to face whatever problems come next. I still have a strong drive to keep creating good work. It just might not be about programming anymore, and figuring that out is what I need to learn and think through in this next stage.

That’s all for this post. Thanks for reading. I hope you’ll give clice a try, and feel free to report any problems!

item.title: 'Birdbrain' Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can

‘Birdbrain’ Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can

In a recent experiment, crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys.

Lemmy and Iggy, two carrion crows, are no strangers to a psychology lab. As study participants, they have helped scientists prove that birds can use tools to forage, learn numbers and count objects, and provided other insights into the ways birds think.

Now, they’ve also revealed that birds can make staggeringly quick decisions, besting their human and nonhuman primate counterparts with ease. In new findings published in Science, the crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys, quantifying the neural speed of avian decision-making for the first time.

The discovery might be the final blow for the use of “birdbrains” as a pejorative.

“We wouldn’t think of birds making these decisions faster than monkeys, or faster than us ‘awesome’ human beings,” said Mike Colombo, a neuroscientist and comparative psychologist at the University of Otago in New Zealand who was not involved in the research. “But they do. They’re just incredibly fast.”

Questions of bird intelligence have long been debated by researchers. Their small and superficially simple brains led scholars in the 19th and much of the 20th century to conclude they were not cognitively competent creatures. Even early research into birdsong, which demonstrated that some birds are capable of complex speech-like patterns and impressive vocal mimicry, was not enough to turn the tide. Their elaborate melodies were considered specialized adaptations that didn’t reflect their cognitive abilities.

Although passionate birders may find those conclusions obviously mistaken, the scientific community has been slower to catch on. “It’s taken the last 20 years to realize that actually their brain architecture is quite fascinating,” said Dr. Colombo.

Recent research, for example, has found that pigeons are capable of distinguishing between cancerous and noncancerous cells, numerical values, and words and non-words. Corvids (the group that includes crows, ravens, rooks and scrub jays) can even recognize themselves, solve abstract problems, plan for the future and show theory of mind — an ability to understand what other birds might be thinking and act accordingly.

item.description:
Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook.

Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt.

Reizungen der Atemwege

Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte.

Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15.

Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus.

Überhöhter Chlorgehalt

Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht.

item.title: Eclipse Mosquitto – An open source MQTT broker
item.description:
Mosquitto is an open source implementation of a server for version 5.0, 3.1.1, and 3.1 of the MQTT protocol. It also includes a C and C++ client library, the mosquitto_pub mosquitto_rr, and mosquitto_sub utilities for publishing and subscribing, and the mosquitto_ctrl, mosquitto_signal, and mosquitto_passwd applications for helping administer the broker.

See the following links for more information on MQTT:

Community page: http://mqtt.org/ MQTT v3.1.1 standard: https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v3.1.1/mqtt-v3.1.1.html MQTT v5.0 standard: https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v5.0/mqtt-v5.0.html

Mosquitto project information is available at the following locations:

Main homepage: https://mosquitto.org/ Find existing bugs or submit a new bug: https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/issues Source code repository: https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto

There is also a public test server available at https://test.mosquitto.org/

See https://mosquitto.org/download/ for details on installing binaries for various platforms.

If you have installed a binary package the broker should have been started automatically. If not, it can be started with a very basic configuration:

mosquitto

Then use mosquitto_sub to subscribe to a topic:

mosquitto_sub -t 'test/topic' -v

And to publish a message:

mosquitto_pub -t 'test/topic' -m 'hello world'

Note that starting the broker like this allows anonymous/unauthenticated access but only from the local computer, so it's only really useful for initial testing.

If you want to have clients from another computer connect, you will need to provide a configuration file. If you have installed from a binary package, you will probably already have a configuration file at somewhere like /etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf. If you've compiled from source, you can write your config file then run as mosquitto -c /path/to/mosquitto.conf.

To start your config file you define a listener and you will need to think about what authentication you require. It is not advised to run your broker with anonymous access when it is publicly available.

For details on how to do this, look at the authentication methods available and the dynamic security plugin.

Documentation for the broker, clients and client library API can be found in the man pages, which are available online at https://mosquitto.org/man/. There are also pages with an introduction to the features of MQTT, the mosquitto_passwd utility for dealing with username/passwords, and a description of the configuration file options available for the broker.

Detailed client library API documentation can be found at https://mosquitto.org/api/

To build from source the recommended route for end users is to download the archive from https://mosquitto.org/download/.

On Windows and Mac, use cmake to build. On other platforms, just run make to build. For Windows, see also README-windows.md.

If you are building from the git repository then the documentation will not already be built. Use make binary to skip building the man pages, or install docbook-xsl on Debian/Ubuntu systems.

cJSON - required c-ares (libc-ares-dev on Debian based systems) - optional, enable with WITH_SRV=yes libedit - for mosquitto_ctrl interactive shell - optional, disable with WITH_EDITLINE=no libmicrohttpd - for broker http api support - optional, disable with WITH_HTTP_API=no openssl (libssl-dev on Debian based systems) - optional, disable with WITH_TLS=no pthreads - for client library thread support. This is required to support the mosquitto_loop_start() and mosquitto_loop_stop() functions. If compiled without pthread support, the library isn't guaranteed to be thread safe. sqlite3 - for persistence support in the broker - optional, disable with WITH_SQLITE=no uthash / utlist - bundled versions of these headers are provided, disable their use with WITH_BUNDLED_DEPS=no xsltproc (xsltproc and docbook-xsl on Debian based systems) - only needed when building from git sources - disable with WITH_DOCS=no

Equivalent options for enabling/disabling features are available when using the CMake build. It is also possible to enable/disable building of specific plugins in the CMake build.

You can download and install mosquitto using the vcpkg dependency manager:

git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git cd vcpkg ./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh ./vcpkg integrate install ./vcpkg install mosquitto

The mosquitto port in vcpkg is kept up to date by Microsoft team members and community contributors. If the version is out of date, please create an issue or pull request on the vcpkg repository.

Mosquitto was written by Roger Light roger@atchoo.org. There have been substantial contributions by other people in the community both in terms of code and other help.

item.title: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy
item.description:
Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy

PMTiles is a tile format which works via HTTP Range requests and can be deployed as a single file to a storage bucket.

I came across Protomaps in research for my latest project, Mapboard.1 For most non-commercial projects, commercial APIs become prohibitively expensive if you ever go viral (Mapbox, for instance, charges $5 per 1k map loads once youâve exhausted the free tier).

PMTiles, part of the Protomaps ecosystem, is a tile format that ships in a single file, accessible via Range requests, and is thus extremely portable and easy to deploy. For CDNs that support caching Range requests of large files, it requires no effort besides down- and uploading it to storage. For others, like Cloudflare, you can utilize an edge function to translate between the traditional x/y/z URL path and Range requests.

Getting some Maps

If all you want is the world map, getting it is as simple as going to the build page and downloading the latest daily build.

However, more fun can be had with the CLI. For example, you can extract data for only a bounding box or specific zoom levels, to get a significantly smaller file.

Deploying to Bunny.net

One great CDN for deploying this is Bunny.net (affiliate link). They support HTTP Range requests, donât collect personal data by default,2 are headquartered in the EU, and offer low-cost access to a global network of CDN and edge storage servers.

Pricing varies based on region and replication factor of the edge storage. But generally you pay $0.01/GB ($0.005/GB on the smaller Volume network) for bandwidth to Europe and North America, and $0.01/GB/month (no replication) to $0.055/GB/month (maximum replication) for storage. A high degree of replication mostly matters for latency in case of a cache miss (as the data is further replicated when itâs cached at the CDN PoPs).

In practical terms, storing the 139GB world map with replication to most continents (5x) will run you about $5/month in storage fees. Loading a map of Europe on a laptop and zooming in on a city causes about 5MB of data to be transmitted, which would be $0.00005 â further navigations and reloads will be less expensive as more of the map gets cached locally. At $0.05/1k map loads that could be 100x cheaper than Mapbox. However, the actual bandwidth of course varies (less for people that bounce immediately, possibly tens of MB for heavy users). For Mapbox you only pay a flat fee per visit.

Uploading the file

Itâs a good idea to create a storage zone with S3 compatibility enabled, as uploading via the HTTP API timed out after 15 minutes for me.

Then, with rclone installed, you can download and stream the file to the Bunny storage zone. Preferably in tmux or from a temporary VPS, if your connection isnât great.

rclone config create bunnycdn s3 \ provider=Other \ access_key_id="<zone-name>" \ secret_access_key="<storage-key>" \ endpoint="https://<primary-region>-s3.storage.bunnycdn.com" rclone copyurl "<build-url>" "bunnycdn:<zone-name>/<filename>.pmtiles" \ --s3-chunk-size 256M \ --progress Configuring the pull zone

Theoretically, at this point you just need to create a pull zone, select the storage zone as an origin, and youâre done. Practically, it would be sensible to change some settings.

Allowed CORS origins can be configured under Security > General > Allowed referrers, so that other websites cannot embed your tiles.

Youâll also want to verify under Caching that âOptimize for large object deliveryâ is enabled, as this makes it possible to cache Range requests.

You might also want to dissuade people from downloading the whole file and leaving you with a large CDN bill. The most practical way Iâve found for this is limiting the download speed to 10kB/s after 10MB transmitted in a single request (using the âDownload speed limitsâ and âLimit afterâ settings under âNetwork limitsâ). Regular usage should never reach this amount. You may further want to introduce a requests/second limit (do note that legitimate usage can also quickly reach high numbers here) or a monthly bandwidth limit for the pull zone.

Embedding the Map

With the tiles deployed, the only thing left to do is to embed them in your website via MapLibre GL, for example. To do this, youâll need to install the pmtiles npm package and add the protocol and a style to MapLibre as detailed in the official installation guide.

Congratulations, you now host your own cost-effective and highly available map of the world!

item.title: Vulcan rocket fails during return-to-flight launch, 40 Amazon satellites lost
item.description:
Vulcan Centaur rocket fails during return-to-flight launch, 40 Amazon satellites lost (video)

United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.

The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today, 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."

Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)

ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.

That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.

Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 15 with news of liftoff, then again at 1:45 p.m. ET with news of the anomaly and loss of the mission.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. Old Bitly Links Are Being Hijacked
item.description:
Update, 15 November, 23:40 UTC: CNN reports redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense as well. Our third check of the Trump links, at 23:35 UTC, found nothing new: 49 links re-created years after their tweets still work.

Update, 15 November, 22:30 UTC: Bitly has confirmed the problem. In a post on X at 19:13 UTC it said it had identified an issue that “allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links” and send people to unrelated content. Bitly said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse.

Update, 15 November, 19:30 UTC: The Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect. Both were still working at 15:05 UTC and returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page by 19:22 UTC. The same has happened to the two extra Trump links we verified and to six of the seven links in our sample that pointed somewhere new. The seventh now shows a Bitly warning that the account that created it has been suspended. The 49 re-created links that look like the originals still work.

Burger King’s X account was not hacked. A Bitly short link in a tweet the chain posted on 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s list of Nazi concentration camps. The tweet was advertising a restaurant locator. A post quoting it passed 2 million views within hours, and Burger King’s original has since become unavailable.

It was not the only one. Eighteen minutes earlier a Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered the same way and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Ransomnews also checked 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, taken from a public archive. Bitly’s own link pages show that 56 were created after the tweets they sit in, and a 57th is blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam. Four were registered on 15 November. Two more, created in January 2024 and January 2025, point at domains that copy the names of crypto services.

In brief Burger King posted the tweet on 24 July 2011 with the short link bit[.]ly/19BFiM. Bitly’s information page for that link gives a creation time of 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 and a destination on Wikipedia. A link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011, bit[.]ly/mLWJO0, was created again at 05:14 UTC the same morning, 18 minutes before Burger King’s. It opens Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Both tweets have since become unavailable. Nobody posted from either company’s account. The links changed hands on Bitly’s side, so the old tweets send readers wherever the new owners choose. Of 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, 40 are still the original. Another 49 were created again later but lead where the tweets suggest, 48 of them in a 17-minute run on 26 May 2023. Seven lead somewhere else and one is blocked by Bitly. Four of those seven were registered on 15 November 2026 between 07:49 and 09:57 UTC. They open a Roblox profile, a YouTube video (twice) and a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. One Trump tweet from April 2011 carries three links to videos of his children. All three have been replaced. Bitly’s help pages say the ending of a bit.ly link cannot be reused, even after the account behind it is deleted. In February 2025 it was reported to have fixed a bug that allowed this. We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November. By 19:22 UTC both links returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. None of the seven Trump links that pointed somewhere new redirects any more. Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC. It said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. CNN reported the same evening that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense were affected too. We have not checked those links ourselves. Was Burger King hacked?

No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s account and nothing suggests anyone got into it. The tweet is 15 years old and reads as it always did, pointing followers to “our handy restaurant locator” through a Bitly link. What changed is where that link goes. As with the Microsoft 365 outage three days earlier, the first question people asked was whether it was an attack on the company, and the answer is the same.

Bitly keeps a public information page for every short link. Add a plus sign to the end of the address and it shows where the link points and when it was created. For bit[.]ly/19BFiM that page gives the destination as Wikipedia’s “List of Nazi concentration camps” and the creation time as 15 November 2026, 05:32 UTC. A link printed in a tweet from 2011 can only carry a 2026 creation date if the same ending was issued a second time.

We tested the method on links nobody disputes. A link whose creator says he made it in 2009 shows a 2009 creation date. A custom link tweeted by a YouTube channel on 21 June 2017 shows 20 June 2017. Among the Trump links that are still original, 32 of 40 were created on the day of the tweet or the day before.

The post that spread it came from an X user at 06:51 UTC, 79 minutes after the link was created, and had 2.2 million views by early afternoon.

By 13:45 UTC the Burger King post inside it was showing as unavailable. We do not know whether Burger King removed it or X did. The short link was still redirecting to Wikipedia at 13:47 UTC.

Was McDonald’s hacked?

No. Its link was changed 18 minutes before Burger King’s. On 7 June 2011 McDonald’s tweeted a Bitly link to something its team in Sweden had done. Bitly’s information page for bit[.]ly/mLWJO0 shows the link was created at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026, and it redirects to Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. The tweet was returning a not-found error when we checked at 14:20 UTC.

The two changes are close in time and alike in style. The X user Alex Greenland, who spotted both timestamps, thinks one person or group is probably behind them. Nothing we have seen proves that.

How does an old Bitly link get hijacked?

Someone registers its ending again. The part of a Bitly link after the slash is called the back-half. Bitly generates one at random, or the user types a custom one. If an old link stops existing and its back-half can be claimed, whoever claims it decides where every tweet, email, PDF and printed QR code carrying that link now leads. No password is stolen and no account is touched, so the brand that posted the link sees nothing wrong.

Bitly says this cannot happen. Its help page on deleted accounts states that bit.ly links keep working and that their back-halves “cannot be re-used”, whether they were generated or custom. A separate page says Bitly deletes accounts that have been inactive for three years. The creation dates we collected do not fit the first statement. Back-halves that appear in tweets from 2009 to 2012 belong to links created between 2023 and today.

It has happened before. In February 2025 Disruptionist reported that memecoin promoters had taken over Bitly links in 2013 posts by Donald Trump and Melania Trump and pointed them at token listings. According to that report, a bug let people claim a back-half once the original link or its account had been deleted or deactivated, and Bitly fixed it and switched off the hijacked links. Links created on 15 November 2026 show the same thing is possible now.

The X user Damin Toell identified it as link hijacking at 07:25 UTC and noted that old Trump posts were affected too.

At 09:18 UTC another user described the method in a post that has been viewed more than 46,000 times. Three more Trump links were registered in the 40 minutes that followed.

Free tool

How does your own site score?

Run the same forty passive checks against your own domain: TLS and certificates, security headers, SPF and DMARC, cookies before consent, and what your stack quietly reveals. A grade out of 100 in about fifteen seconds.

No signup. Nothing installed. We only request what your site already serves publicly.

How many old links have been replaced?

More than half of the ones we tested. We took every tweet Donald Trump’s account posted from 2009 to 2016 from the Trump Twitter Archive data set on GitHub, left out retweets and extracted the bit.ly links. That gave 97 different links, first used between 2009 and 2013, with 61 of them from 2011. We chose this account because its old posts were named in the reports of 15 November and in the 2025 case, and because a full public archive exists. For each link we recorded where it redirects and the creation date on Bitly’s information page, at about 13:45 UTC on 15 November 2026.

Forty links are untouched. Forty-nine were created again later and lead to addresses that fit the tweets: mostly videos on Trump’s YouTube channel, plus pages at CNBC, CNN and the Wall Street Journal. Forty-eight of those were created between 14:55 and 15:12 UTC on 26 May 2023, roughly one every 20 seconds. We do not know who did that. It looks like a repair job by someone who knew where each link used to go, and it means those back-halves were free to claim by May 2023.

That leaves eight links that now lead somewhere their tweets never pointed.

Tweet date What the tweet promoted Link created again Where it goes now 3 Jun 2009 An iGoogle page 15 Nov 2026, 07:49 UTC A Roblox user profile 1 Jul 2010 A golf course in Scotland 15 Nov 2026, 09:36 UTC A YouTube video 17 Sep 2010 A QVC jewellery show 15 Nov 2026, 09:47 UTC The same YouTube video 7 Oct 2010 A golf course in Scotland 15 Nov 2026, 09:57 UTC Wikipedia’s article on Trump and Jeffrey Epstein 14 Mar 2011 A video blog 29 Jan 2025, 21:09 UTC test[.]com 25 Apr 2011 A video of Donald Trump Jr. 18 Jan 2025, 21:43 UTC worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com 25 Apr 2011 A video of Eric Trump 17 Jan 2024, 11:08 UTC dappradars[.]website 25 Apr 2011 A video of Ivanka Trump Not shown Blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam
One tweet, three replaced links

On 25 April 2011 the account posted three Bitly links to “The Next Generation” videos of Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump and Eric Trump. The first now leads to worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com, a domain that borrows the name of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture. The third leads to dappradars[.]website, one letter away from the crypto analytics site DappRadar, at a path named “eligibility/check”. Bitly blocks the second with a notice that it was “flagged as redirecting to malicious or spam content”.

WHOIS records from WhoisXML API show both domains were registered afresh after the links were created. The current registration of dappradars[.]website began at 02:56 UTC on 15 November 2026, through Hostinger, although the Bitly link that points there was created in January 2024. The domain now forwards to a YouTube video. The current registration of worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com dates from 11 April 2026, through Namecheap, almost 15 months after the link was created, and its HTTPS certificate failed verification when we checked. We have not seen what either domain served when the links were first made.

A replaced link can be replaced again. When the domain behind it lapses, the next buyer inherits whatever traffic the old tweet still sends.

More Trump links outside our 97

X users found replaced Bitly links in Trump tweets from 2012 and 2013 that the archive stores only as t.co addresses. We checked two. The link in a tweet of 10 January 2013 was created at 23:52 UTC on 14 November 2026 and opens a page on Steam. The link in a tweet of 10 September 2012 was created at 01:04 UTC on 15 November and opens a YouTube video. Late on 14 November is the earliest change in this wave that we have seen.

Which re-created links still work?

We ran the same check on the 97 Trump links twice more, at 19:25 and 23:35 UTC on 15 November. The seven links that pointed somewhere new no longer redirect. The other 49 links created years after their tweets still do: 48 were made within 17 minutes of each other on 26 May 2023 and one in February 2025. They point to what look like the original pages, mostly YouTube videos and news articles. We do not know who re-created them or why. The 40 original links work as before.

How we counted

We used the archive’s condensed yearly files for 2009 to 2016 and found bit.ly links only in tweets up to 2013. From late 2011 Twitter wrapped links in its own t.co shortener, and the archive stores most later links in that form (1,218 of them in 2012), so Bitly links behind those are not among our 97. A link counts as created again when Bitly’s information page shows a creation date more than 30 days after the first tweet that used it. In practice the gap was at least 11 years in every case. Destinations were read from the redirect header without opening the pages. The count covers one account and one link shortener. It shows that these links were claimed. How many of Bitly’s older links can be claimed is something only Bitly can answer. Domain registration data is from WhoisXML API.

Who else was affected?

CNN reported on the evening of 15 November that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense carried redirected Bitly links too, along with a 2013 post from McDonald’s Indonesia account. It counted at least a dozen in Trump’s posts, in a wave that appears limited to posts from 2009 to 2014. Burger King told CNN it had nothing to do with the redirects.

We have not checked those links ourselves. Bitly was already disabling affected links when they were reported, and a disabled link no longer shows when it was created. The accounts we verified directly are Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump.

What happened on 15 November 2026?

The first change we found came late on 14 November. The McDonald’s and Burger King links followed at 05:14 and 05:32 UTC the next morning. All times below are UTC and on 15 November unless stated.

Saturday 14 November: the earliest change we found 23:52 Link takenA link in a 2013 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a page on Steam, the earliest change we found. Sunday 15 November, morning: the brand links are taken 01:04 Link takenA link in a 2012 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a YouTube video. 02:56 Domaindappradars[.]website, the target of a Trump link replaced in 2024, is registered afresh. 05:14 Link takenThe back-half in McDonald’s 2011 tweet is registered and pointed at Wikipedia. 05:32 Link takenThe back-half in Burger King’s 2011 tweet is registered and pointed at Wikipedia. 06:51 XAn X user quotes the Burger King tweet. The post goes on to pass 2 million views. 07:25 XAnother user identifies it as link hijacking and says old Trump posts are affected. 07:49 Link takenA link in a 2009 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a Roblox profile. 09:18 XA user describes the method in public. 09:36 to 09:57 Links takenThree links in 2010 Trump tweets are registered. Sunday 15 November, afternoon and evening: Bitly responds 13:45 Burger KingBurger King’s post shows as unavailable. Its link still redirects to Wikipedia. 14:20 McDonald’sMcDonald’s post returns a not-found error. Its link still redirects to Wikipedia too. 15:05 Our checkBoth links still redirect to Wikipedia. 19:13 BitlyBitly says on X that an issue let old, inactive links be repurposed, that it has suspended the accounts involved and that it is disabling the affected links.Why it matters: this is the first confirmation from Bitly that old links could be taken over. 19:22 Our checkBoth links return Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. So do six of the seven Trump links in our sample that pointed somewhere new and the two we verified outside it. The seventh shows a warning that the account that created it has been suspended. 21:10 CNNCNN reports redirected links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense. 23:35 Our checkOur third check finds no further change. Forty-nine re-created links in the Trump sample still redirect. Status NowThe Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect, and neither do the Trump links that pointed somewhere new. Forty-nine re-created links in the Trump sample still work. Bitly has not said how many links were taken. Checked at 23:35 UTC on 15 November. Why does a joke link matter?

Because the same move works for fraud. The examples from 15 November are pranks: a Wikipedia page, a game profile, a video. The 2025 wave pushed memecoins, and two of the Trump links in our table lead to domains named after crypto services. A link inside an old post from a verified brand, a bank, a ministry or a news outlet carries that account’s credibility, and X shows the post exactly as it was written. Readers have no reason to doubt it.

The exposure is wider than X. The same short links sit in old emails, PDFs, slide decks, printed QR codes and help pages. Security researchers file this under broken link hijacking: a link outlives the thing it pointed to, and someone else moves in.

What should brands and readers do?

Any organisation that posted short links years ago should assume some of them are no longer its own.

List the short links in your old posts. Export your post archive from each platform and pull out every bit.ly address. Check each one. Add a plus sign to the link and compare Bitly’s creation date with the date of your post. A later date means the link is no longer yours. Remove what you cannot fix. Delete posts whose links were replaced or no longer resolve, and report replaced links to Bitly. Use a short domain you own for new links, so nobody else can issue the same address.

For everyone else, the checks take a few seconds.

Do not trust a link because the post is old or the account is verified. The account owner may have no control over where it goes. Preview before you click. Adding a plus sign to a bit.ly link shows the destination without visiting it. Be most careful with pages that ask you to sign in or connect a crypto wallet. What happens next?

Bitly has to say whether old back-halves can still be claimed and what it will do about the ones already taken. We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November. Later that day the links that pointed somewhere new were deactivated, and 49 others created years after their tweets were left working. Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC and said it was still disabling affected links. Its statement does not say how many links were taken or how. Checks like this one are what our breach verification desk is for, and we will update this article when either company responds or the numbers move.

Frequently asked questions Was Burger King hacked in November 2026?

No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s X account. A Bitly short link in a tweet from 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026, so the old tweet began sending readers to a different page.

Was McDonald’s hacked?

No. A Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered again at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Nothing was posted from the McDonald’s account.

Why did a Burger King tweet link to a list of Nazi concentration camps?

The tweet’s Bitly link, bit[.]ly/19BFiM, originally advertised a restaurant locator. Bitly’s information page shows the link was created again at 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 with a Wikipedia article as its destination. Burger King did not choose that destination.

What is Bitly link hijacking?

It is when someone registers the ending of an old Bitly link that no longer exists and points it at a page of their choice. Every old post, email or document that carries the link then leads to the new destination. No account is broken into.

How can I tell whether a Bitly link has been replaced?

Add a plus sign to the end of the link. Bitly shows the destination and the date the link was created. If the creation date is later than the post or document the link appears in, the link is not the original.

Were Donald Trump’s old tweets hacked?

No. Ransomnews checked 97 Bitly links in tweets from 2009 to 2013. Fifty-six were created again after the tweets were posted and one is blocked by Bitly. Seven of them lead to destinations unrelated to the tweets, including two domains that copy the names of crypto services.

Has Bitly fixed the problem?

A fix was reported in February 2025 after links in Trump posts were pointed at memecoin pages. Links created on 15 November 2026 show that old endings can be claimed now. Bitly had made no public statement that we could find by 14:30 UTC that day. It confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC and said it was disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse.

Who else was affected by the Bitly link hijacking?

CNN reported redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense, as well as Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump. Ransomnews verified the Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump links directly.

Are the hijacked Bitly links still active?

The ones we tracked are not. By 19:22 UTC on 15 November 2026 the Burger King and McDonald’s links, and the Trump links that pointed somewhere new, returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. Bitly said it was still disabling affected links, so check any old short link before you trust it.

item.title: Show HN: The Last Complication, a Zachtronics-style watchmaking puzzle game
item.description:
Thirty houses, counted down the first row, back up the second and down the third. The strip beside the board is the week: ten throws, taken in order, and then again from the top.

A throw moves one counter exactly that many houses. One counter to a house, and none may pass two that stand together.

Every counter stops on the 26th house. The 27th is water: a counter that lands there goes back to the 15th. A counter leaves the board by the exact count.

If a counter can move, one must. A throw that none can use is left over, and the game is lost.

The bench is laid out for a tall screen.

item.title: Preserving 30 Years of Salon Journalism
item.description:
When Salon launched in 1995, the web was still finding its voice. One of the first major publications born on the internet, Salon helped define a new kind of digital journalism, bringing together politics, culture, criticism, and ideas for a generation of online readers.

After 31 years, Salon has announced that it is ceasing publication. But thanks to web archiving, the stories don’t have to disappear.

The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been preserving Salon for nearly three decades—the online publication has been published over time at salon1999.com, salonmag.com and, since 1999, salon.com. Today, more than 250,000 Salon articles can be discovered through the Wayback Machine, representing a record of digital journalism and the conversations that shaped our culture since the earliest days of the web.

To make exploring this web archive easier, we’ve also launched an experimental Salon Explorer, a new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism. Browse more than 250,000 articles and explore the work of over 20,000 writers using filters that make it easier to find stories and discover writing you may have missed.
